_readme: SAIRNlaw deadline engine seed -- Indiana civil litigation (Indiana Rules of
Trial Procedure). Phase 3, state jurisdiction #2 of 4 (OH/IN/MI/PA).
Indiana only in this file -- one state at a time, verified before the next.
Every value below was read from the official current rule text at
rules.incourts.gov or from the Indiana Code on 2026-08-22 and is quoted in
the row. Nothing was carried over from the Ohio seed or the federal seed on
the assumption that a similar-looking rule is the same rule.
FINDING 1 -- THE SUBSECTION LETTERS IN CIRCULATION ARE STALE, AND CITING
THEM WOULD HAVE BEEN WRONG. Secondary sources (law-firm articles, practice
guides, and several search results) consistently cite 'T.R. 6(C)' for the
twenty-day response deadline and 'T.R. 6(E)' for the mail extension. The
CURRENT official rule text does not match that. Verified twice against
rules.incourts.gov with verbatim quoting, because a first partial read of
the same page disagreed with a second full enumeration -- the disagreement
itself is why it was re-checked rather than accepted:
(A) Computation
(B) Automatic Enlargement of time
(C) Other Requests for Enlargement of time
(D) Response and Reply Deadlines   <-- the twenty-day rule
(E) Time to serve motions
(F) Affidavits
(G) Additional time after service by United States mail   <-- the
three-day mail extension
(H) Dissolution Actions--Sixty-day waiting period
(I) Local Rules Abrogated
This is the same failure shape already flagged for Pennsylvania (competing
rule numbers from different sources) -- it turned out to be real here too,
on a state that was not flagged for it in advance.
FINDING 2 -- INDIANA'S SHORT-PERIOD EXCLUSION LOOKS LIKE OHIO'S AND IS NOT
THE SAME RULE. Both use a seven-day threshold, so a copy-from-Ohio would
have produced the right threshold for the wrong reason and the wrong
exclusion set. Ind. T.R. 6(A): 'When the period of time allowed is less
than seven days, intermediate Saturdays, Sundays, legal holidays, AND DAYS
ON WHICH THE OFFICE IS CLOSED must be excluded from the computations.' The
office-closed limb has no Ohio or federal analog. THIS ENGINE DOES NOT
MODEL IT -- there is no field anywhere for a particular clerk's office
closures, and inventing one would mean guessing at facts about a specific
courthouse. Its absence errs in the SAFE direction (one fewer day excluded
produces an EARLIER date, never a later one), but it is a real limitation,
stated here rather than left implicit. The same limb appears in the
last-day rollover text of 6(A) and is likewise not modelled.
FINDING 3 -- INDIANA'S HOLIDAY LIST IS NOT THE FEDERAL LIST AND NOT OHIO'S.
IC 1-1-9-1 was read directly. Real differences, none assumed:
* ABRAHAM LINCOLN'S BIRTHDAY, February 12, is an Indiana legal holiday.
No federal or Ohio analog.
* GOOD FRIDAY is an Indiana legal holiday -- 'a movable feast day'. Its
date is computed, not looked up: 2026-04-03 and 2027-03-26, each
independently confirmed against published calendars after computing it.
* JUNETEENTH IS ABSENT from IC 1-1-9-1's enumerated list, even though it
is on both the federal and Ohio calendars already loaded here. It is
NOT included below. This is the single most likely thing to be wrong by
assumption in the whole file, so it is called out rather than quietly
matching the other two states.
* SHIFT RULE differs from Ohio's. IC 1-1-9-1(b): 'When any of these
holidays, other than Sunday, comes on Sunday, the following Monday
shall be the legal holiday. When any of these holidays comes on
Saturday, the preceding Friday shall be the legal holiday.' Indiana
shifts BOTH directions, like the federal calendar. Ohio shifts only
Sunday. Applied per date below, checked by day-of-week, not copied.
* 'Sunday, the first day of the week' is itself listed as a legal holiday
in IC 1-1-9-1. Not enumerated as dates below -- the engine already
treats every Sunday as non-countable via its weekend handling, and
listing 52 Sundays a year would be a second mechanism for the same
fact.
FINDING 4 -- ELECTION DAY IS A LEGAL HOLIDAY AND CANNOT BE FULLY
ENUMERATED. IC 1-1-9-1 makes a legal holiday of 'Election Day, the day of
any general, municipal, or primary election'. Statewide dates are
verifiable and ARE included (2026 primary 2026-05-05, 2026 general
2026-11-03, both confirmed). MUNICIPAL elections vary by locality and
cannot be enumerated for the whole state from here, so the 2027 municipal
primary and general dates are NOT included. A missing holiday causes the
engine to under-roll, producing an EARLIER date than the true deadline --
the safe direction -- but any Indiana computation landing near a local
election day should be checked by hand.
FINDING 5 -- THE MAIL EXTENSION IS NOT ATTACHED, AND THE REASON IS WEAKER
THAN OHIO'S. Ohio's Civ.R. 6(D) carved out responses to service of summons
in its own text, so omitting it there was certain. Indiana's T.R. 6(G) has
NO SUCH EXPLICIT CARVE-OUT. Its scope is 'within a prescribed period after
the service of a notice or other paper' served by United States mail. A
summons and complaint that commences an action is served under T.R. 4,
while T.R. 5 governs service of 'pleadings, documents, and other papers' in
a pending case -- so whether 6(G) reaches the initial answer deadline is a
genuine open question that was NOT resolved from primary sources here.
Secondary sources assert both readings. NO service_extension is attached to
the rule below, which is the FAIL-SAFE choice: omitting an extension that
does apply produces a date three days EARLIER than the true deadline, while
attaching one that does not apply produces a date three days LATER -- the
direction that loses a right. This is an unresolved legal question flagged
for a human, not a settled encoding.
ALSO OBSERVED, NOT ENCODED: T.R. 6(B) gives a party 'one automatic
thirty-day enlargement of time to respond to a complaint or other pleading
by filing a notice with the court'. That is a party ACTION, not a
computation -- it changes the deadline only once someone actually files the
notice, which is a case fact this engine is not given. Encoding it as an
automatic +30 would produce a date a month too late for every party who
never filed one. Recorded here because it is a large, real, Indiana-
specific feature that a future phase may want to model as an explicit
user-supplied event.
STILL OPEN, NOT IN THIS FILE: Michigan MCR 1.108 and Pennsylvania (the
Pa.R.C.P. 106 vs. 201 Pa. Code Sec. 107 conflict is still unresolved).

rules.label: Response to a pleading after service (Indiana)

authority.quote: A response to a pleading must be filed within twenty days after service of the pleading.
authority.note: Cited as 6(D)(1) from the CURRENT official rule text, not the 6(C) that secondary sources still repeat -- see _readme finding 1. No service_extension attached: whether T.R. 6(G)'s three-day mail extension reaches an initial answer deadline is a genuine unresolved question (T.R. 4 service vs. T.R. 5 'notice or other paper'), and omitting it errs three days EARLY rather than three days LATE -- see _readme finding 5. The office-closed limb of 6(A) is not modelled -- see _readme finding 2. effective_from is the Indiana Trial Rules' original adoption date (1970-01-01, per the official rules PDF's own title, 'Indiana Rules of Trial Procedure Adopted, January 1, 1970'); the twenty-day figure's own amendment history back to 1970 was NOT independently traced, and a November 2023 proposed-amendments document plus a 2025 rules order both exist and were not fully read, so a matter triggered in an earlier era should have the then-current text confirmed by hand.

Shifts BOTH Saturday (to preceding Friday) and Sunday (to following Monday), unlike Ohio's Sunday-only shift. Independence Day 2026 falls on a Saturday and IS shifted to Friday 2026-07-03 under IC 1-1-9-1(b) -- matching the federal calendar here but for Indiana's own statutory reason, not by inheritance. Includes Abraham Lincoln's Birthday (Feb 12) and Good Friday, which have no federal analog. EXCLUDES Juneteenth, which is absent from IC 1-1-9-1's list despite being on the federal and Ohio calendars. Statewide election days included; municipal election days are not enumerable statewide and are omitted -- see _readme finding 4.

dates.name: Independence Day (observed, July 4 falls on Saturday)

authority.note: Loaded alongside 2026 so a period triggered late in 2026 does not refuse for a missing year. Independence Day 2027 falls on a Sunday and shifts to Monday 2027-07-05; Christmas Day 2027 falls on a Saturday and shifts to Friday 2027-12-24 -- both under IC 1-1-9-1(b)'s two-way shift, each checked by day-of-week. Good Friday 2027 computed as 2027-03-26 and confirmed against published calendars. NO election days are listed for 2027: Indiana's municipal elections fall in odd years and vary by locality, so they cannot be enumerated statewide from here -- an Indiana computation in 2027 landing near a local election day must be checked by hand. See _readme finding 4.
